Second-Quarter Financial Highlights Net sales of $1,557 million; year-over-year increase of 20.4% Net income of $233 million and net income per diluted share of $4.85 Non-GAAP diluted EPS increased year-over-year to $6.35 Adjusted EBITDA increased year-over-year to $431 million Recorded IEEPA tariff recoveries of $73 million, of which $14 million received in the quarter Share repurchases of $268 million “Our record results reflect broad-based demand for our innovative solutions and excellent execution on our growth and profitability priorities. We delivered for our customers by leveraging our long-standing supplier relationships to support our growth," said Bill Burns, Chief Executive Officer of Zebra Technologies. "The momentum we see across our business underscores Zebra's position as the foundation for intelligent operations and frontline AI as customers digitize and automate environments." "Our strong balance sheet and cash flow continue to provide significant financial flexibility, enabling us to invest for growth while returning more than $560 million to shareholders in the first half of the year through disciplined share repurchases," said Nathan Winters, Chief Financial Officer of Zebra Technologies. "We believe this balanced approach positions Zebra to create long-term shareholder value." Download PDF with consolidated balance sheet, cash flow and income statements Second Quarter 2026 Compared to the Second Quarter 2025 Net sales were $1,557 million compared to $1,293 million in the prior year. Net sales in the Connected Frontline ("CF") segment were $903 million compared to $717 million in the prior year. Asset Visibility & Automation ("AVA") segment net sales were $654 million compared to $576 million in the prior year. Consolidated organic net sales increased 9.2% year-over-year, with a 7.5% increase in the CF segment and an 11.4% increase in the AVA segment. Gross profit was $825 million compared to $616 million in the prior year. Gross margin increased to 53.0% compared to 47.6% in the prior year primarily due to IEEPA tariff recoveries and favorable foreign currency exchange. Adjusted gross margin was 53.3% compared to 47.9% in the prior year. Operating expenses increased to $504 million from $433 million in the prior year primarily due to expenses associated with acquired businesses including amortization of intangible assets. Adjusted operating expenses increased to $419 million from $370 million in the prior year. Net income was $233 million, or $4.85 per diluted share, compared to net income of $112 million, or $2.19 per diluted share, in the prior year. Non-GAAP net income increased to $305 million or $6.35 per diluted share, compared to $186 million, or $3.61 per diluted share for the prior year. Adjusted EBITDA increased to $431 million, or 27.7% of adjusted net sales, compared to $267 million, or 20.6% of adjusted net sales in the prior year. Balance Sheet and Cash Flow As of July 4, 2026, the Company had cash and cash equivalents of $157 million and total debt of $2,776 million. For the first six months of 2026, net cash provided by operating activities was $387 million and the Company invested $26 million in capital expenditures, resulting in free cash flow of $361 million. The Company also made share repurchases of $568 million. Outlook Mr. Burns added, "Strong demand momentum and progress on productivity and memory supply supports our significantly increased outlook for the full year. We are focused on driving sustainable growth across our business with our innovative portfolio of solutions, as we continue to benefit from trends in automation and Physical AI." Third Quarter 2026 The Company expects third quarter sales growth between 17% and 20% compared to the prior year. This expectation includes approximately 10.5 points of favorable impact from business acquisitions, dispositions and foreign currency. Adjusted EBITDA margin for the third quarter is expected to be approximately 22%. Non-GAAP diluted earnings per share are expected to be in the range of $4.70 to $4.90. This assumes an adjusted effective tax rate of approximately 19%. Full Year 2026 The Company expects full year sales growth between 14% and 16% compared to the prior year. This expectation includes approximately 8 points of favorable impact from business acquisitions, dispositions and foreign currency. Adjusted EBITDA margin for the full year is expected to be between 23.5% and 24.0%. Non-GAAP diluted earnings per share are expected to be in the range of $20.75 to $21.25. This assumes an adjusted effective tax rate of approximately 19%. Free Cash Flow for the full year is expected to be greater than $1 billion. title: Waymo Is Growing Faster Than Ever. So Are Its ‘Edge Cases.’
summary: As Waymo deploys more driverless cars to 15 U.S. cities and counting, its vehicles keep encountering new and unexpected situations that they have no script to handle.
body_text: You have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load. Waymo driverless cars are in San Francisco and 14 other metropolitan areas, including Denver, Las Vegas, San Diego and Tampa. Credit... Jason Henry for The New York Times Supported by SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Listen · 9:14 min By Emmy Martin Reporting from San Francisco Aug. 10, 2026 On July 4, more than 100,000 people packed San Francisco’s waterfront for a foggy fireworks show over the Golden Gate Bridge. When they tried to go home, Waymo got in the way. With crowds milling around, Waymo’s driverless cars blocked intersections and choked traffic. Some drivers were stuck behind the electric robo-taxis for more than three hours. Several Waymos had to be towed after their batteries died in the gridlock. At least two drove over exploding fireworks, with one catching fire. Rose Peterson was inside the other. She and her fiancée had ordered a Waymo to return to their hotel. When the car stopped at an intersection, a man ran into the road, set a firework on the street and lit it. The Waymo drove forward, rolling over the firework as it exploded beneath the car. Video Rose Peterson and her fiancée were inside a Waymo driverless car on July 4 when it ran over a firework that someone had set off on the street. Credit Credit... Video by Rose Peterson “We were just in absolute shock,” said Ms. Peterson, 30, who works in insurance in Walnut Creek, Calif. The car smelled like it was on fire, she said, but the Waymo kept going until it stalled at another intersection. She and her fiancée then got out and walked the rest of the way to their hotel, turning what was supposed to be a five-minute drive into an hourlong journey. What Ms. Peterson experienced is what the driverless car industry calls an “edge case,” which are the unscripted situations that no one trained the robo-taxis to handle. The problem is that edge cases appear to be piling up as Waymo, the leading autonomous car service, rapidly expands. Thank you for your patience while we verify access. body_text: More tools won't free your nights. Here's the coordination architecture that lets operators run 35 properties at a 96% AI automation rate without being on call. Airbnb automation means replacing manual, repetitive tasks with software that handles guest communication, pricing adjustments, cleaning coordination, and check-ins without you doing the work personally. But the real purpose of short-term rental automation is structural: it breaks the direct connection between your portfolio size and your personal hours. Without that break, every property you add doesn't just add revenue, it adds proportional work. See our AI for hospitality for how this works in practice. Hosts in the Airbnb Community forum report spending anywhere from a few hours to 20-plus hours per week per property on hosting and admin tasks, and that number compounds fast across multiple listings. The failure point is usually invisible until you're already stuck. Most short-term rental owner-operators believe that incomplete automation is a tool-count problem: they just haven't found the right combination of apps yet, and once they do, the gaps will close on their own. At one property, manual management feels manageable. At two or three, coordination overhead starts compounding, a cleaning handoff gets missed, a late-night check-in question arrives at 11pm, a pricing window closes while you're handling something else. Hosts report operational overwhelm right around this threshold, which is why most solo operators never scale past it. The familiar approach is to stack tools: one app for messaging, another for pricing, a third for cleaning tasks. But the gaps between those tools still require a human to catch failures, route exceptions, and make judgment calls. Hosts who have tried AI for hospitality platforms describe the same realization: the missing piece isn't another app, it's a coordination layer that knows how their business runs. Erwan Le Roy, operating 35 properties under the Cash Flow Street brand, reached a 96% AI automation rate, verified through Conduit's platform analytics, not by accumulating more tools, but by giving an AI agent access to his actual SOPs and guest protocols. 96% AI automation rate across 35 properties Key takeaways Airbnb automation isn't about convenience, it's structural: the only way to grow your portfolio without growing your hours is to break the link between property count and personal time. Most operators mistake an incomplete automation stack for a tool-count problem, but five apps running in parallel still leave a human in the middle catching every handoff the tools can't coordinate. Erwan Le Roy's 35-property operation hit a 96% AI automation rate, not by adding more apps, but by giving one coordination layer access to his actual SOPs, guest protocols, and operating knowledge. The 18 automation layers covered here span pricing, guest messaging, cleaning coordination, dynamic check-in, and review management, but the architecture matters more than any individual tool. Automation ROI isn't a monthly cost question; it's a 'what is manual handling costing me right now' question, and most operators are underestimating both sides of that math. conduit.ai's AI Agents close the final gap by reading directly from your SOPs, manuals, and FAQs to handle guest conversations across every channel, accurately, autonomously, and without a human on standby. Why Most Airbnb Automation Stacks Hit a Ceiling: and What Operators Are Missing Stacking more tools rarely closes the gaps that keep operators tethered to their phones, because the real problem is not the number of apps running but the absence of anything connecting them. Each point solution automates one slice of a workflow in isolation, leaving you as the only node in the system that holds enough context to handle anything those tools were not explicitly built for. Understanding where that coordination breaks down is the first step toward building an operation that does not route every edge case back to you. Why Your Current Automation Stack Still Leaves You on Call at Midnight Most short-term rental owner-operators believe that incomplete automation is a tool-count problem: they just haven't found the right combination of apps yet, and once they do, the gaps will close on their own. Five tools running in parallel can feel like a solved problem. The pricing algorithm adjusts nightly rates, the message scheduler fires check-in instructions, the smart lock generates codes, and the cleaning app pings your housekeeper after checkout. Yet every stack has a gap: a missed notification, a guest question no template covers, a situation that falls precisely between two tools and routes straight back to you. The critical difference between task automation and operational freedom is coordination. Each point solution in a typical short-term rental stack automates one slice of a workflow in isolation. The pricing tool does not know what the messaging tool just sent. The smart lock does not know the cleaner marked the unit as not ready. When a guest messages at midnight asking whether early check-in is possible given a delayed cleaning job, no individual tool holds enough context to answer. That question lands in your inbox because you are the only node in the system that holds all the information. As Darren, Founder of Easy BnB / Bali Luxury Stays, puts it after making the shift: "We all agree that AI first is the best approach", because coordination has to be built into the foundation, not bolted on afterward. Where Automation Gaps Hide, and How to Plug Them Before They Leak Revenue We all agree that AI first is the best approach Late-night booking inquiries are the clearest example of where fragmentation costs money. No automated message template was triggered because the guest has not booked yet. Nobody in the stack owns the pre-booking conversation, so the inquiry sits unanswered until morning, when the guest has already booked somewhere else. The revenue leak is structural, not accidental, a direct consequence of building a stack where each tool's ownership ends at the edge of its own function. This problem is most acute for operators using AI messaging tools and AI for hospitality platforms, where the volume of pre-booking, mid-stay, and post-stay messages makes a manual response cadence impossible to sustain without someone being effectively on call around the clock. The fix is not another message template. It is an AI Agent trained on your existing documentation, your SOPs, FAQs, and house manuals, that can answer any guest question continuously, before, during, or after a stay, without waiting for a human to intervene. Conduit's AI Agents are built for exactly this purpose. Critically, connecting that documentation requires no IT or developer work: the operator or ops lead connects the docs directly, and the first automated guest reply is live within days of connecting those materials. Why Adding More Apps Won't Break Your Automation Ceiling, and What Actually Does The familiar response is to add another tool, a Zapier workflow, a new integration, a smarter scheduler. But the ceiling is not a tool-count problem; it is a coordination problem ). What closes the gap is a unified layer that sits across your existing stack, reads the context those tools generate, and acts on it coherently. That is the role Conduit's Integrations layer plays. It is most valuable when your business already uses tools like Notion, Google Drive, or Airbnb and you want the AI agent to leverage that existing content without manual re-entry. The operator links the accounts, no IT or developer needed. The knowledge your team has already built lives where it always has; the AI agent simply gains access to it. From there, Workflows handle the recurring, predictable guest touchpoints that currently require a manual staff action: a booking confirmation follow-up a check-in reminder a post-stay review request Workflows fire after a trigger event in a conversation or guest lifecycle: after a booking is confirmed, after check-in, or when a specific keyword is detected. The operator or ops lead sets the rules; no IT needed. And the Inbox gives the operations or support team a single place to monitor, review, and manage every conversation the AI agent is handling across all platforms and properties, ongoing visibility without constant intervention. Together, these four layers, AI Agents, Inbox, Workflows, and Integrations, replace the coordination gap that no individual point solution can close. You can read more about how STR operators are auditing their current automation stack to identify exactly where these gaps live before they leak another season of revenue. 18 Ways to Automate Your Airbnb Business - The Full Automation Architecture Operators who hit 90% automation rates don't have more tools than everyone else. They have a better architecture. That distinction matters because the instinct most hosts follow, find a new app for every friction point, produces a stack that looks impressive in a spreadsheet and still requires a human in the middle to catch the handoffs. The tools automate their own slice. Nobody automates the space between them. The 18 methods below are organized as a layered architecture, not a flat list. The first layer builds the operational foundation. The second handles discrete tasks in isolation. The third shapes the guest experience. The fourth, the one most operators never build, is the coordination intelligence layer that holds your operating knowledge and closes the gaps every other tool leaves open. Each layer compounds the one beneath it. Skip a layer and the whole structure leaks. Automation Stack Decision Checklist - Which Layer Should You Build First? Use this checklist before purchasing any new tool. A 'yes' to every item in a layer means you're ready to move to the next. 1. Conduit.ai - Best All-in-One Airbnb Automation Platform Conduit.ai centralizes the full automation stack for Airbnb hosts, guest messaging, pricing, task dispatch, and review management, under one AI-driven dashboard. It's the right pick for hosts managing 3+ listings who want to eliminate tool-switching overhead. The one real tradeoff is that its breadth means a steeper onboarding curve compared to single-purpose tools. 2. Automated Guest Messaging with Triggered Sequence Templates Automated guest messaging is the biggest daily time drain for most hosts who haven't addressed it. A properly configured sequence covers booking confirmation, pre-arrival instructions, check-in day reminders, a mid-stay check-in, checkout instructions, and a post-stay review request, all sent at the right interval without manual action. Platforms like Hospitable and most PMS tools handle this well for the predictable 80 percent of guest interactions. A lockout that requires a judgment call exposes a gap that is structural, not a configuration problem. 3. Dynamic Pricing Automation via Algorithmic Rate Tools Dynamic pricing tools like PriceLabs, Wheelhouse, or AirDNA's own rate recommendations automatically adjust your nightly rate based on local demand signals, competitor occupancy, seasonality, and lead time. For hosts in competitive markets, this alone can lift revenue 15–40% over flat pricing. The core limitation is that algorithms can misprice during hyperlocal events unless you set manual overrides. 4. Smart Lock Integration for Keyless Automated Check-In Connecting a smart lock, August, Schlage, or Yale, directly to Airbnb generates unique guest access codes automatically for each reservation window and revokes them at checkout. This eliminates key handoffs entirely and is the foundational automation for any host who wants to operate remotely. The tradeoff is upfront hardware cost and the need for a reliable Wi-Fi connection at the property. 5. Automated Cleaning Dispatch with Turno (formerly TurnoverBnB) Turno syncs directly with your Airbnb calendar and automatically creates a cleaning job the moment a checkout is confirmed, notifying your cleaner with the exact turnover window. It handles cleaner payment, photo verification, and damage reporting in one flow. For hosts managing multiple properties, this replaces a spreadsheet entirely. The fee per property adds up at scale, but the time savings justify it for most operators. 6. Centralized Multi-Listing Calendar Sync Across OTAs Using a channel manager or iCal sync to unify your Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com calendars prevents double-bookings and gives your entire team, cleaners, co-hosts, maintenance, a single source of truth. This is the connective tissue that makes every other automation reliable. The limitation is that iCal sync has a 15–30 minute delay, making real-time channel managers worth the cost for busy listings. 7. Automated Review Request and Response Workflows Scheduling an automated post-checkout message that thanks guests and gently prompts a review, sent within 2 hours of checkout, consistently lifts review rates. Pairing this with templated host review submissions for guests closes the loop without manual effort. The risk is that a generic review request sent after a problematic stay can backfire, so smart hosts add a conditional logic filter for flagged reservations. 8. Property Management Software (PMS) as the Automation Hub A full PMS like Hostaway, Guesty, or Lodgify acts as the central nervous system connecting pricing, messaging, cleaning, and reporting into one platform. For hosts with 5+ listings, a PMS pays for itself by replacing 4–6 separate subscriptions. The tradeoff is monthly cost and the time investment to configure it properly, hosts with 1–2 listings often find it overkill. 9. Automated Noise and Occupancy Monitoring with NoiseAware NoiseAware and similar sensors monitor decibel levels continuously and send automated alerts when noise exceeds thresholds, letting you intervene before neighbors complain or property damage occurs. This is a critical automation layer for urban properties or those in HOA communities. The important caveat is that these devices must be disclosed to guests per Airbnb policy, and improper placement can create privacy concerns. 10. Automated Upsell and Early Check-In Offer Sequences Triggered messages sent 48–72 hours before arrival can automatically offer guests early check-in, late checkout, or local experience add-ons for a fee. When the property is available, this converts dead time into incremental revenue with zero manual effort. The limitation is that Airbnb's native messaging doesn't support payment collection for upsells, requiring a third-party tool or direct payment workaround. 11. Automated Inventory and Restocking Alerts via Checklist Apps Requiring cleaners to complete a digital checklist after each turnover, logging consumable levels like toiletries, coffee pods, and paper goods, creates an automated low-stock alert system. Tools like Turno and Properly support photo-verified checklists that flag shortages before the next guest arrives. The tradeoff is that this only works if your cleaning team consistently completes the digital checklist rather than skipping it. 12. Zapier-Powered Custom Automation Workflows Between Tools Zapier and Make (formerly Integromat) let hosts build custom automation bridges between tools that don't natively integrate, for example, triggering a Slack notification to a co-host when a new booking lands, or logging every reservation into a Google Sheet for tax tracking. This is the power tool for hosts who want bespoke workflows without coding. The limitation is that complex multi-step Zaps require troubleshooting when APIs change. 13. Automated Pricing Floor and Ceiling Rules with Seasonal Overrides Beyond basic dynamic pricing, setting hard minimum and maximum price rules, plus seasonal override blocks for holidays and local events, ensures algorithms never price your listing below profitability or above market tolerance. This rule-based guardrail layer is what separates hosts who profit from dynamic pricing from those who get burned by it. The tradeoff is that overly tight floors can reduce occupancy during slow periods. 14. Automated Tax Collection and Remittance via Avalara MyLodgeTax Avalara MyLodgeTax and similar services automatically calculate, collect, and remit occupancy taxes to the correct jurisdictions based on your property location and booking dates. For hosts in states or cities where Airbnb doesn't collect taxes on their behalf, this automation eliminates significant compliance risk. The cost is a monthly subscription plus a percentage of taxes remitted, which is negligible compared to penalty exposure. 15. AI-Powered Guest Screening and Booking Approval Automation Tools like Autohost and Superhog automatically screen incoming booking requests against risk signals, profile completeness, review history, ID verification status, and either approve, flag, or decline them without host intervention. This is essential for hosts who use Instant Book but want a safety net. The limitation is that automated screening can occasionally flag legitimate guests, requiring a manual review override process. 16. Automated Financial Reporting and Owner Statement Generation For co-hosts and property managers handling owner properties, tools like Hostfully and Guesty automatically generate monthly owner statements showing revenue, expenses, cleaning fees, and management commissions. This eliminates hours of manual spreadsheet work and builds owner trust through transparency. The tradeoff is that accurate statements depend on all expenses being logged in the system, manual expense entries are still required for off-platform costs. 17. Smart Thermostat Automation for Energy Cost Control Integrating a Nest or Ecobee thermostat with your booking calendar automatically sets energy-saving temperatures during vacant periods and restores guest-comfortable settings before each arrival. For properties in climates with extreme temperatures, this can cut utility costs by 20–30% annually. The limitation is that guests can override thermostat settings during their stay, so some hosts add a temperature range lock via the thermostat's app. 18. Automated Post-Stay Damage Detection with AI Photo Comparison Emerging tools like Properly and Minut's damage detection features use AI to compare post-checkout cleaner photos against a baseline property photo set, automatically flagging new damage for host review. This creates a timestamped evidence trail that strengthens Airbnb AirCover claims. The current limitation is that AI detection accuracy still requires human confirmation before filing a claim, making it a triage tool rather than a fully autonomous system. The real question is not "what does this cost per month?" but "what is it costing me to go without it?" Both sides of that equation belong in the same spreadsheet. Airbnb Automation Tool Costs by Category - Realistic Ranges for Each Layer of Your Stack Airbnb automation cost varies significantly by category. A property management system (PMS) typically runs $20 to $50 per unit per month at the entry tier, scaling with channel count and feature depth. Dynamic pricing tools such as PriceLabs, Wheelhouse, and Beyond price between $19 and $30 per listing per month depending on portfolio size and billing structure. Smart locks are a one-time capital expense averaging $150 to $300 per door, with no recurring SaaS fee. Stacked together, a full automation layer for a five-property portfolio runs $300 to $600 per month before factoring in any AI-powered communication layer. The same dynamic plays out at scale. Haven operated 270 properties and needed approximately 25 support staff across multiple shifts to handle check-in questions, lockouts, cleaning issues, and complaints. When Conduit was installed, the team was running at only 40% automation with no workflows and a minimal knowledge base, enough to reduce message volume at the margins, but not enough to change how the team operated. Every new property added more messages, more calls, and more headcount. Growth, without a fully configured AI communication layer, was simply proportional hiring. This is where a unified guest communication layer earns its place in the stack. The key isn't accumulating more point-solution tools; it's giving an AI agent access to your actual SOPs and guest protocols so it can handle coordination across your entire stack, not just isolated tasks. Why bother investing in Airbnb automation if my current tool stack already covers the basics? A stack of individual tools still requires a human to catch handoffs, route exceptions, and make judgment calls in the gaps between them, which is why hosts report operational overwhelm right around the two-to-three-property threshold and most solo operators never scale past it. The missing piece isn't another app; it's a coordination layer that holds all your operating context and acts on it coherently, which is what an AI agent trained on your existing documentation provides. How do smart locks actually help with automating check-ins? Smart locks generate unique, time-sensitive access codes for each guest automatically, tied to reservation start and end times, so check-in instructions go out without any human involvement. The most common failure point is integration lag, when the lock's code-delivery system and your messaging automation run on separate timers, guests can receive check-in instructions before their code is active, which is why choosing a lock that integrates directly with your PMS matters. Are noise monitors allowed on Airbnb, and do I have to tell guests about them? Airbnb's policy requires hosts to disclose noise monitoring devices, and guests who discover undisclosed monitoring tend to leave reviews that are difficult to recover from. Devices like Minut track decibel levels without recording audio; disclosing them upfront and framing them as a community-courtesy measure means most guests accept them without friction.

title: Acadia Realty Trust Announces $0.20 Per Share Quarterly Dividend
summary: The Investor Relations website contains information about Acadia Realty Trust's business for stockholders, potential investors, and financial analysts.
body_text: RYE, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 5, 2026-- Acadia Realty Trust (NYSE:AKR) (“Acadia” or the “Company”) today announced that its Board of Trustees has authorized a cash dividend of $0.20 per common share for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. The quarterly dividend is payable on October 15, 2026 to holders of record as of September 30, 2026. About Acadia Realty Trust Acadia Realty Trust is an equity real estate investment trust focused on delivering long-term, profitable growth. Acadia owns and operates a high-quality real estate portfolio of street and open-air retail properties in the nation's most dynamic retail corridors (“REIT Portfolio”), along with an investment management platform that targets opportunistic and value-add investments through its institutional co-investment vehicles (“Investment Management”). For further information, please visit www.acadiarealty.com . The Company uses, and intends to use, the Investors page of its website, which can be found at https://www.acadiarealty.com/investors , as a means of disclosing material nonpublic information and of complying with its disclosure obligations under Regulation FD, including, without limitation, through the posting of investor presentations and certain portfolio updates. Additionally, the Company also uses its LinkedIn profile to communicate with its investors and the public. Accordingly, investors are encouraged to monitor the Investors page of the Company's website and its LinkedIn profile, in addition to following the Company’s press releases, SEC filings, public conference calls, presentations and webcasts.
